```{r}
#| include: false
source("_helper.R")
```

A vellumplot plot is a specification, not a picture, and that is not only a
statement about when the drawing happens. The spec is *plain data* — a nested list
of encodings, scales, coordinates, facets, labels, and page size — which means it
can be written to a file, sent over a wire, diffed, generated by something that is
not you, and compiled somewhere else.

```{r}
p <- vplot(mtcars, width = 6.5, height = 4) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl), size = 2.4) |>
  labs(title = "Weight against mileage", x = "weight (1000 lbs)", y = "mpg",
       color = "cylinders")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
vg(p, "spec-as-data")
```

`summary()` reports the structure without drawing anything:

```{r}
#| message: true
summary(p)
```

## Round-tripping through JSON

`spec_to_json()` writes it out and `spec_from_json()` reads it back:

```{r}
json <- spec_to_json(p)
substr(json, 1, 320) |> cat()
```

```{r}
p2 <- spec_from_json(json)
identical(plot_manifest(p)$spec_hash, plot_manifest(p2)$spec_hash)
```

The spec hash is unchanged, so the recompiled plot is the same plot — not a plot
that resembles it.

What matters more than the round-trip working is what happens when it *cannot*
work. The spec covers the subset of the grammar a portable document can carry
faithfully; anything outside it — a custom transform function, a pattern fill,
hand-drawn `sketch()` geometry, a secondary axis, per-layer data — is **refused**
with an error naming the exact slot, rather than dropped on the floor and
discovered later by looking at the picture:

```{r}
#| error: true
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_bar(x = factor(cyl), fill = pattern_stripe()) |>
  as_spec()
```

Data is inlined when it is small and stored by reference — name, content hash,
column schema — when it is not, in which case `from_spec(spec, data = )` supplies
it back at compile time.

## Checking a spec before compiling it

`spec_diagnose()` validates a spec against a dataset and returns a verdict instead
of throwing. Every referenced field is checked against the data, then the spec is
dry-run compiled:

```{r}
broken <- sub('"field": "wt"', '"field": "weihgt"', json, fixed = TRUE)
d <- spec_diagnose(broken, data = mtcars)
d$ok
str(d$diagnostics, max.level = 2)
```

A misspelled field comes back as a record — severity, which field, and what the real
ones are — rather than a traceback. That is the shape a generator can act on: whatever wrote
the spec, whether a person or a program, gets told what to fix. `vplot_from_spec()`
is the strict form, raising a classed error carrying the same diagnostics.

## Handing it to another grammar

Vega-Lite is also a layered grammar of graphics, so most of a spec maps across
directly:

```{r}
vl <- spec_to_vegalite(p)
vl$mark
str(vl$encoding, max.level = 2)
```

And the same principle applies at the boundary: what the bridge cannot express is
*reported*, not quietly changed. A polar plot has no Vega-Lite equivalent, so the
translation says which features it dropped:

```{r}
#| warning: true
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_bar(x = factor(cyl)) |>
  coord_polar() |>
  spec_to_vegalite() |>
  names()
```

That is the throughline of all of it: the spec is data you can inspect, store, and
program against, and every place it loses something it says so. See
[A figure that carries its own provenance](provenance.qmd) for the hashing side of
the same substrate.
